what: XSS (cross-site scripting) is when an attacker gets their script to run on your page. Defence is layered: frameworks escape output by default, a sanitiser cleans any HTML you must render, Trusted Types lock the dangerous DOM sinks, and a strict Content Security Policy (CSP) blocks scripts you did not approve.
like: Like a school with a visitor sign-in desk: staff check every guest (escape and sanitise), only badged people enter certain rooms (Trusted Types), and the front-door rules say which adults may speak to the class at all (CSP).
why: One XSS bug lets an attacker act as the user: read the page, call APIs, and steal anything JavaScript can reach
CSP limits the damage when a bug slips through - defence in depth
Frameworks are safe by default, so most XSS now comes from escape hatches and third-party scripts

nodes.t: Untrusted input|user text, URL, API data
Trusted Types|sinks only accept typed values

steps.d: Anything from users, URLs, query params, third-party APIs or the CMS can carry markup. The rule: render data as text, never as HTML.
React, Vue and Angular escape by default, and textContent never parses markup. The risks are escape hatches: dangerouslySetInnerHTML, v-html, innerHTML, and javascript: URLs.

steps.t: Sanitise when you must render HTML
steps.d: For rich text, run it through DOMPurify with a strict allow-list, and do not modify the string after sanitising.

steps.t: Lock the sinks with Trusted Types
steps.d: With require-trusted-types-for 'script', assigning a plain string to innerHTML throws. Only values made by a named policy (which calls your sanitiser) are accepted.
Send a per-response nonce (or hashes) with strict-dynamic, object-src 'none' and base-uri 'none'. Inline handlers, javascript: URLs and eval are blocked unless allowed.
Ship Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only first, collect reports through report-to, fix what breaks, then enforce.

numbers.l: Trusted Types object kinds: TrustedHTML, TrustedScript, TrustedScriptURL
Trusted Types is 'Newly available' across the latest browsers since February 2026
XSS kinds: stored, reflected and DOM-based

choices.d: Nonces need server-rendered HTML with a fresh random value per response (hard on pure static hosting). Hashes suit static pages but must be regenerated on every script change.

Host allow-lists are easy to bypass and hard to maintain. A nonce plus strict-dynamic lets trusted scripts load their own dependencies; the trade-off is that a trusted script that builds script tags from attacker input is still dangerous.
Sanitise at render time with the context in mind (OWASP): encoding for HTML text, attribute and URL contexts differ. Storing pre-sanitised HTML makes later policy changes hard.

choices.t: Enforce Trusted Types now or later
choices.d: Start report-only to find all sink writes, use the default policy only as a migration aid, then enforce with an allow-list of policy names.

instead.why: HttpOnly cookies and a BFF limit what a successful XSS can steal
What JavaScript can read is exactly what XSS can steal

breaks.d: dangerouslySetInnerHTML or innerHTML with user content, or a user-supplied URL put in href.
breaks.see: Injected script or javascript: link in a comment or profile field
breaks.fix: Sanitise with DOMPurify, validate URL schemes to http and https, lint for the escape hatches

breaks.d: A tag manager or CDN script is changed and runs with full page power.
breaks.see: Unexpected requests or DOM changes from a vendor script
breaks.fix: Subresource Integrity, minimal third-party scripts, CSP, and isolate in sandboxed iframes where possible

breaks.d: A new CSP blocks inline styles, analytics or an extension.
breaks.see: Blank widgets and CSP violation reports after a release
breaks.fix: Report-only first, monitor reports, then enforce; keep a quick rollback for the header

say: Our first line is that data is always rendered as text; the framework escapes by default and we lint for dangerouslySetInnerHTML and innerHTML.
Where we must show rich HTML we sanitise with DOMPurify behind a Trusted Types policy, so any raw string reaching a dangerous sink throws.
On top we send a nonce-based strict CSP with strict-dynamic, object-src none and base-uri none, rolled out report-only first, as defence in depth and not the primary defence.

followups.q: Is CSP enough to stop XSS?
followups.a: No. OWASP calls it an extra layer because mistakes are easy; escaping, sanitising and safe APIs prevent the bug and CSP reduces the impact.
Client script reads input such as the URL and writes it to a sink like innerHTML. Trusted Types are aimed at this class because they make every sink write go through a policy.

followups.q: How do you add CSP to an existing app?
followups.a: Start with Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, collect violations through report-to, fix inline code and third parties, and then enforce, ideally with nonces rather than allow-lists.

today: A nonce plus strict-dynamic policy is the recommended CSP shape, and Trusted Types reached Baseline 'Newly available' status in 2026, so enforcing them is now practical for new apps. React 19 blocks javascript: URLs in href and src, but OWASP still advises validating URLs yourself.

check.a: Makes DOM sinks like innerHTML reject plain strings
check.why: Only TrustedHTML, TrustedScript or TrustedScriptURL objects from a policy are accepted, else a TypeError is thrown.

check.q: Why must a CSP nonce differ on each response?
check.a: If it is predictable, an attacker can include it in injected script
d: Browsers cache nonces for one request only
Nonces are used to sign cookies
check.why: The nonce is the secret proving a script came from the server.

check.q: Best handling for user comments containing limited HTML?
check.a: Sanitise with a library like DOMPurify before rendering
d: Strip the word script with a regex
Encode once at write time and trust it forever
Put it in a hidden iframe without sandbox
check.why: Regex filters are bypassable; a maintained sanitiser with an allow-list is the OWASP recommendation.
